passage: The diploma project report was due at the government polytechnic on Friday, and Naveen had already rewritten the introduction three times. On Wednesday evening, sitting on the cot outside his father's grocery shop in Hunsur, he pointed at the wall clock. "Till nine. Then I stop." His friend Suraj came by with two glasses of tea. "Still on page one?" "Page twelve. At nine I'm printing it." At nine the water-pump diagram was still slightly crooked and one table had no borders. Naveen turned over an old bill and wrote: "Next time: draw diagrams first, check tables early." Then he carried the report to the photocopy shop before its shutter came down. On Friday the lecturer handed it back with "Good, clear work" and one comment about the diagram. Naveen tucked the old bill into his file.

qa.q: What did Naveen write on the back of the old bill?
qa.a: He wrote "Next time: draw diagrams first, check tables early."

qa.q: Why might stopping at nine have felt hard for Naveen even though the report was nearly done?
qa.a: He had already rewritten the introduction three times, so part of him believed one more pass would make it safer; stopping with a crooked diagram meant accepting it was not perfect.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday evening turned things around for Naveen?
qa.a: Fixing nine o'clock as a firm stop and printing then, while writing down fixes for next time, let him hand in a solid report instead of polishing forever.

qa.q: How might Suraj see Naveen's new way of working?
qa.a: Suraj half expected him to be stuck on page one, so seeing Naveen finish on time and still get "Good, clear work" would likely surprise and please Suraj.

grounding: It shows a student who stops at a fixed hour, submits a solid report and notes improvements for next time, keeping high standards without getting stuck.

passage: Sunday, four o'clock, and the essay on the 1918 flu was due at midnight. Nkechi had been fiddling with her opening paragraph since breakfast. Her flatmate Hana, making toast, watched her delete the same sentence twice. "What's the plan?" Hana asked. Nkechi took a breath. "Two more hours. Then references, then I submit, whatever it looks like." She put her phone on the other side of the kitchen and set the oven timer. When it rang at six, the conclusion felt thin and she still wanted a better quote in section two. She opened a note titled "Essay 4" and typed: start reading earlier, collect quotes as I go. At 7:40 she pressed submit. Hana raised her mug. Three weeks later the essay came back with a 68 and a comment: "Strong argument; conclusion could go further." Nkechi added that line to her note too.

qa.q: What did Nkechi use to time her last two hours?
qa.a: She set the oven timer.

qa.q: What does Nkechi deleting the same sentence twice suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stuck and uneasy, as if the opening had to be exactly right before she could move on, even with the deadline hours away.

qa.q: What would you advise Nkechi to do with the "Essay 4" note before her next assignment?
qa.a: Read it on the first day and act on it early, for example collecting quotes while reading, so the high standard is built in from the start instead of patched at the end.

qa.q: What was it like for Hana to watch Nkechi delete the same sentence twice?
qa.a: Hana could see her flatmate losing a whole day to one paragraph, so asking about a plan was a light way to help without taking over.

grounding: It shows a student who gives the essay a time limit, submits a solid version and records what to improve next time, so high standards do not become paralysis.

passage: Disha, you keep reopening that slide deck. Sit a minute. Your Anand mama was exactly like this at twenty-four, at the insurance office in Nagpur. Every claims report I wrote, I went through again. Then again. Commas, column widths, one more cross-check. My manager wanted the monthly summary on the fifth; I'd send it on the ninth, spotless. Meanwhile Joshi from the next desk sent his on the fourth, a bit rough, and in the review meeting the boss said, "Joshi is our fast one." Nobody remembered that my figures had been perfect. I missed my cousin's sangeet because of one report. Your mami, before we married, once waited an hour for me at the bus stand. Good work matters, beta. But a report that comes late helps nobody, and I paid for all that polish with sleep and with people.

qa.q: When did Anand send the monthly summary that was due on the fifth?
qa.a: He would send it on the ninth, spotless.

qa.q: Why did checking every report again and again feel right to young Anand?
qa.a: He believed spotless figures proved he was careful and good at his job, so each extra cross-check felt like protection against mistakes.

qa.q: At what point could young Anand have chosen differently, and what might that choice have been?
qa.a: Once the summary was solid by the fifth, he could have sent it on time and kept a short list of small fixes for the next month, instead of holding it four more days.

qa.q: How might Anand's future wife have felt waiting an hour at the bus stand?
qa.a: She probably felt let down and a little unimportant, left waiting while a report came first.

grounding: An elder recalls polishing every report until it was late while a faster colleague got the praise, showing how rigid standards cost time, rest and relationships.

passage: The donor report was due at five, and the Wi-Fi in the NGO's cramped Bhopal office kept dropping every twenty minutes. Hansa had finished her section on Monday. It was now Thursday. She was still re-colouring the charts, rewording the summary, checking figures she had already checked. Arohi, who sat opposite, had uploaded a share of the report at noon: a few typos, but done. At three the director stopped by. "Arohi, thanks for getting it in early. Very helpful." Hansa kept her eyes on the screen. Her phone buzzed: her sister, asking about dinner, the third missed call that week. She let it ring. At 4:52, with the connection finally holding, she pressed send, then sat back with a headache beside a lunch box she had never opened.

qa.q: At what time had Arohi uploaded a share of the report?
qa.a: Arohi had uploaded it at noon.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep her eyes on the screen when the director thanked Arohi?
qa.a: She likely felt a sting of hurt and unfairness, having worked longer and more carefully yet going unnoticed, and did not want it to show on her face 😔

qa.q: What could Hansa try on the next report once her section is finished?
qa.a: She could allow one final check with a fixed cut-off, send it early, and keep a short list of small improvements for later.

qa.q: How might Hansa's sister see the week of missed calls?
qa.a: Her sister may feel pushed aside and a bit worried, since three calls went unanswered and dinner plans stayed unclear.

grounding: Under a deadline and a failing connection, an adult keeps polishing finished work while a quicker colleague gets thanked, showing the time, rest and relationship costs of rigid standards.

passage: Noa had booked a table at the ramen place near Umeda for Hiroshi's birthday, but at six he texted: "Sorry, can't. Still fixing the catalogue layout." It was his second cancellation that week. Noa got two portions to take away and climbed the stairs to his flat. Hiroshi opened the door in yesterday's shirt, eyes red. On his screen, the furniture catalogue looked finished to her. "The margins on page nine are off by a millimetre," he said. "And the grey is a bit too warm. I was up till four." Noa set the noodles on his desk. "Can I see it as a draft? Just a good-enough draft. We go through it together for thirty minutes, and whatever's left, you write down and send it anyway." He hesitated, then slid the laptop over. By eight they were eating, and the file was in his client's inbox.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi say was wrong with page nine?
qa.a: The margins on page nine are off by a millimetre.

qa.q: What might Hiroshi have been worried about while he stayed up till four?
qa.a: He was probably afraid the client would spot tiny flaws like the margins or the warm grey and think less of him, even though the catalogue already looked finished.

qa.q: Which move of Noa's helped Hiroshi get unstuck, and why?
qa.a: Calling it a good-enough draft and offering thirty minutes together gave him a limit and company, so sending it felt less risky 🙂

qa.q: How does Noa see the catalogue compared with how Hiroshi sees it?
qa.a: To Noa it looks finished, while Hiroshi sees only the millimetre and the colour; she can see the whole piece that his worry hides from him.

grounding: A friend sees someone cancel plans and lose sleep over tiny flaws, then offers to go through the work together as a good-enough draft.

passage: In the staff canteen of the water-testing lab in Coimbatore, Lakshmi noticed that Sangeeta's idli had gone cold, untouched. Her friend's laptop was open beside the plate, the quarterly sample report on screen. "You're coming to the film tomorrow, no?" Lakshmi asked. "Can't. The graphs don't line up, and two readings show three decimals instead of two." Sangeeta rubbed her eyes. "I slept maybe three hours." It was the same report she had called "almost done" on Monday. Lakshmi pulled her chair round. "Show me. I'll read it like a draft that's allowed to be good enough, not like an inspector. Anything tiny, we put on a sticky note for version two." They went through it before the tea break ended. Sangeeta fixed the decimals, left the graph spacing, and sent it at four. Then she texted Lakshmi: "Film tomorrow. You pick 🙂"

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi notice Sangeeta's untouched idli?
qa.a: In the staff canteen of the water-testing lab in Coimbatore.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta felt worn down by the report?
qa.a: She rubbed her eyes, said she slept maybe three hours and left her idli cold; a small decimal issue had grown into something she could not put down.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta at the canteen table changed how her week went?
qa.a: Letting Lakshmi read it as a good-enough draft, fixing the decimals and leaving the spacing, meant the report went out at four and the film plan was back on.

qa.q: If Lakshmi had just said "It's fine, send it," what might have changed?
qa.a: Sangeeta might not have believed her and kept polishing alone; sitting down and reading it together is what made the leftover imperfections feel survivable.

grounding: A friend notices someone losing sleep and cancelling a plan over tiny flaws and offers to review the work as a good-enough draft together.

passage:
Dear Reena chechi,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Okay, here it is.
At Alan's birthday party on Saturday, everyone was praising the cake and I said, loudly, "Did you get it from the bakery? It tastes bought." His mum had made it herself. She was standing right behind me.
It's Thursday now and I still can't stop. On the bus, in maths, in bed, I play it again. I think of better things I could have said, like if I find the right line I can fix it. But every time, my face goes hot all over again. I'm sure the whole class still remembers. Today Alan asked me for my science notes like normal, and I still thought he was only being polite.
Is this normal? Did you ever do this?
Joseph

qa.q: What did Alan ask Joseph for today?
qa.a: Alan asked for Joseph's science notes like normal.

qa.q: Why does replaying the moment feel useful to Joseph?
qa.a: Joseph feels embarrassed and hopes that finding the right line could somehow fix it, so each replay feels like work on the problem, even though it brings the hot face back every time.

qa.q: What small step could Joseph try when the replay starts on the bus again?
qa.a: Joseph could check the replay against facts, like Alan acting normal, and then turn to something else; one short sorry to Alan's mum could also help close it.

qa.q: How might Alan's mum remember the party compared with Joseph?
qa.a: She may have felt a small pinch in the moment but probably moved on quickly; for her it was one comment on a busy evening, not something to relive all week.

grounding: A teenager keeps replaying an awkward party comment for days, imagining everyone still remembers, while the replaying only deepens the sting.

passage:
Kashish, promise you won't laugh. Remember Tanya's Holi party on Sunday? We were all eating gujiyas on the terrace, and I turned to Mohit and Pari and said, "You two are so cute together." Everyone went silent, because they broke up last week. Everyone knew. Except me. Pari just said, "Um, no, Avni," and walked off to get water.
Since then I keep doing it. In the shower I replay the silence. In chemistry the teacher's voice turns into that terrace. At night I lie there practising what I should have said, like if I get it perfect in my head it'll undo it. It doesn't. It just stings more every time. And I'm sure the whole group chat is still talking about it. Wait. Are they? Be honest.

qa.q: What did Avni say to Mohit and Pari on the terrace?
qa.a: Avni said, "You two are so cute together."

qa.q: Why does Avni keep practising what should have been said?
qa.a: Avni half believes that getting the words perfect could undo the moment, so the replaying feels like fixing it, even though it only stings more 😔

qa.q: What could Kashish say that might help Avni step out of the loop?
qa.a: Kashish could answer the real question honestly, for example that the group chat has moved on, and suggest one short, simple sorry to Pari instead of more rehearsing.

qa.q: How might Pari have experienced the moment on the terrace?
qa.a: Pari was probably caught off guard and a bit sore, which is why Pari walked off for water, but that hurt came mostly from the fresh breakup, not from Avni.

grounding: A teenager who made an awkward remark at a party relives it for days and imagines the group still discussing it, and the reliving deepens the hurt.

passage:
Mentor notes, Jomon Kurian, B.Sc Nursing first year, 18 September
Seema came to my cabin again today, the third time since the anatomy results. She failed the paper by six marks. She doesn't ask what to do about the supplementary exam. She asks why. "Was it the hostel noise? Am I too slow? Maybe I'm not made for nursing, sir." Each visit brings the same questions in a new order, and she leaves looking more tired, not less. She told me she lies awake going over the question paper line by line.
Today I didn't answer the why. I asked her to write down one thing she could do this week. She sat with the pen a long time, then wrote: "Ask Rincy to study the bones chapter with me on Tuesday." I've asked her to come back on Friday and tell me how it went.

qa.q: By how many marks did Seema fail the anatomy paper?
qa.a: She failed the paper by six marks.

qa.q: Why might asking "why" again and again feel important to Seema?
qa.a: She seems to feel that finding the true cause will tell her what the failure means about her, so the questions feel like working on it, even as they wear her down.

qa.q: What turning point did Jomon try to create in today's visit?
qa.a: He stopped answering the why and asked for one thing she could do this week, which moved her from searching for causes to a concrete plan with Rincy.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the pattern in Seema's visits?
qa.a: He notices the same questions returning in a new order and that she looks more tired each time, so he can see the talking is not helping her.

grounding: A student who failed a paper keeps asking why and what it says about her without making any plan, and the questioning leaves her lower each time.

passage:
Friday, 11:40 p.m.
Results came out at noon. Failed Business Law. 31.
I've spent the whole day on one question. Why? Was it the two weeks I gave to the college fest? Was it that I read the cases but never practised writing answers? Or am I just someone who can't handle serious subjects, and everyone was being nice about it until now? Maybe Abba was right that I should have taken science.
Round and round on the bus, in the canteen, in the shower. Every answer I find makes me feel worse, and none of them tell me what to do.
Thomas texted at 9: "reval or supplementary? need help making a plan?" I typed "idk" and put the phone face down.
Still awake. Still asking why.
Noor

qa.q: What did Thomas text Noor at 9?
qa.a: "reval or supplementary? need help making a plan?"

qa.q: Why does Noor keep asking why even though each answer feels worse?
qa.a: Noor seems to hope that finding the real reason will make sense of the failure, so the questioning feels like doing something, but it keeps sliding into judgements about who Noor is.

qa.q: What would you advise Noor to do with Thomas's message tomorrow?
qa.a: Reply yes, sit with Thomas to choose between re-evaluation and the supplementary, and pick one first step, like practising answer writing, so the thinking becomes a plan.

qa.q: What is it like for Thomas to get "idk" back?
qa.a: Thomas made a clear offer and got almost nothing in return, so Thomas may feel shut out and unsure whether to push or give Noor space.

grounding: A student who failed a paper spends the day asking why and what it says about them, reaches no plan, and feels lower as the night goes on.

passage:
Running club notes, Arnab, Thursday
Gopika has been in my batch for three years and is my friend outside it too. Since she missed the qualifying time for the Kolkata half marathon by forty seconds, every cool-down has become the same talk. The cramp at the fifteenth kilometre. The water station she skipped. Whether the watch was wrong. I've listened each time and added my own guesses about the heat.
This week I noticed she leaves these talks slumped, not lighter. We've gone over it nine or ten times and nothing new comes out. Today, instead of another round, I asked gently, "What's one small thing that would help right now?" She was quiet, then said she'd like to plan the next race together. We picked one in March and wrote the first two training weeks on the back of my clipboard sheet.

qa.q: By how much did Gopika miss the qualifying time?
qa.a: She missed it by forty seconds.

qa.q: Why might Gopika keep going over the cramp and the water station?
qa.a: She likely feels that pinning down exactly what went wrong will ease the disappointment, so each retelling seems useful, even though she leaves slumped.

qa.q: What did Arnab change today, and why did it help?
qa.a: Arnab stopped adding guesses and asked about one small thing that would help now, which turned the talk toward planning the March race.

qa.q: How has the repeated talk affected Arnab as the listener?
qa.a: Arnab kept listening and guessing along but came to see that the talks brought nothing new and no relief for Gopika, which is what prompted a different question.

grounding: A friend who keeps going over a disappointment with the same person notices it brings no relief and gently asks what small step would help now.

passage:
Tuesday night
Pema came over again after work. Momos, tea, and the craft fair rejection, round four. The letter said her pottery "didn't fit this year's theme." We went through it all again: was it the photos, the glaze, the fact that the organiser's cousin got a stall? I kept nodding and saying "so unfair," and I meant it.
But tonight I watched her face while we talked. She didn't look better at the end. She looked like she'd walked the same circle again and was more tired from it. Me too, honestly.
So when she paused, I asked, "What's one small thing that might help now, even a tiny one?" She stared at her cup. Then she said, "Maybe I'll sell the new bowls myself, from home." She took three photos of them on my windowsill before she left 🙂
Ira

qa.q: What did the rejection letter say about Pema's pottery?
qa.a: It said her pottery "didn't fit this year's theme."

qa.q: What did Ira notice that suggested the talks weren't helping Pema?
qa.a: Pema didn't look better at the end; she looked as if she had walked the same circle again and was more tired from it.

qa.q: What made Ira's question work where nodding had not?
qa.a: It asked for one small step now instead of more reasons, so Pema could move from the old rejection to photographing the new bowls 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Ira kept saying "so unfair" every night?
qa.a: The two friends would likely keep circling the same complaint; Pema would stay stuck in the disappointment, and Ira might start to dread the visits.

grounding: A friend who has been rehashing someone's disappointment with them notices it gives no relief and gently asks what small step might help now.

passage:
You asked how I got through the month after the pitch, Aditi. Honestly? Badly at first. Every night I'd lie there replaying what the investor said, that my plan was "charming but naive." Round and round till two.
Then my cousin, who's a counsellor, told me something simple: "Zainab, when it starts, catch it." So now I keep a notebook by the stove. I write the thought exactly: "They think I'm naive." I set my phone timer for ten minutes and let myself chew on it properly. When it rings, I close the book and start cooking, something fiddly, like rolling parathas or doing biryani from scratch. My hands get busy, and my head follows.
Some nights it still comes back. But my cousin also said that if it ever stops lifting, or gets really dark, I should see someone properly. I've kept that promise to myself.

qa.q: Where does Zainab keep the notebook?
qa.a: Zainab keeps a notebook by the stove.

qa.q: Why was the investor's comment so hard for Zainab to let go of at night?
qa.a: Zainab felt hurt and belittled by 'charming but naive', which seemed like a verdict on Zainab, so replaying it felt like trying to answer it and kept Zainab awake till two.

qa.q: What makes cooking a good choice after the ten-minute timer rings?
qa.a: Something fiddly like rolling parathas keeps the hands busy so the mind follows, which gives the loop a clear end instead of letting it drift back.

qa.q: Why might the counsellor cousin have added the part about seeing someone?
qa.a: The cousin likely wanted Zainab to know the notebook and timer suit ordinary loops, but thoughts that become constant or dark deserve real professional support.

grounding: An adult catches a ruminating loop, writes the thought down, gives it a short timed slot, then cooks, and keeps professional help in mind if it turns constant or dark.

passage:
I'm Nazia, and I share a flat with Bidisha in Salt Lake. Since her project was handed to someone else at work, I've seen a pattern at night. She'd sit on the sofa staring at the switched-off TV, and when I asked, she'd say, "Just thinking about the meeting again."
Last week something changed. Around nine she took out a small yellow pad, wrote a line I couldn't see, and put her phone on the table with a timer running. She sat with the pad till it beeped. Then she stood up, tied her hair back and said, "Walk?" We did two rounds of the park by the lake. Another night she made shukto from her mother's recipe, humming.
I can't say what's in her head now. But she laughs at dinner again. And I've told her that if it ever gets constant or dark, I'll go with her to a counsellor.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say when Nazia asked about the staring?
qa.a: She'd say, "Just thinking about the meeting again."

qa.q: Why can't Nazia be sure how Bidisha feels now, and what hints are there?
qa.a: Nazia only sees the outside and couldn't read the yellow pad, but the walks, the humming while cooking and the laughter at dinner suggest her evenings feel lighter.

qa.q: Which part of Bidisha's new evening seems to break the loop, and why?
qa.a: Stopping when the timer beeps and moving straight into a walk or cooking shukto gives the thought a set time and then something absorbing to fill the mind.

qa.q: How has Bidisha's change affected Nazia?
qa.a: Nazia no longer comes home to someone staring at a blank TV and can share walks and dinners again, while staying ready to go with Bidisha to a counsellor if things get worse.

grounding: A flatmate observes an adult who writes the looping thought down, gives it a timed slot and then walks or cooks, with a counsellor in mind if it becomes constant or dark.

passage:
Monday night: Ankita lay under the fan, eyes wide open. What if she failed the spelling test? What if Mummy's scooter slipped in the rain on the way home from the clinic? She called out three times. Her mother, Jyoti, came each time, a little more tired.
Wednesday night: Jyoti sat on the bed. "Worries are like a doorbell that rings too much," she said. "Let's make a bedtime plan." Warm milk, one story, then Ankita would say three good things from the day. "And I'll always tell you when I'm home safe."
Saturday night: Ankita heard the scooter, then Mummy's voice from the door: "Home!" She whispered her three good things and fell asleep before the story ended.

qa.q: What three things were in the bedtime plan?
qa.a: Warm milk, one story, then Ankita would say three good things from the day.

qa.q: What was Ankita worried about on Monday night?
qa.a: She was afraid of failing the spelling test and scared that her mother's scooter might slip in the rain on the way home.

qa.q: Which change helped Ankita most, and why?
qa.a: The steady bedtime plan together with Jyoti's promise to say when she was home gave Ankita something calm to hold on to instead of the alarms.

qa.q: What was Monday night like for Jyoti?
qa.a: Jyoti came each time but was tired, and being called three times probably worried her too, which is why a plan helped them both.

grounding: A child's night-time what-ifs about failing and about her mother's safety ease once a calm bedtime routine and a promise of reassurance are in place.

passage:
Gopika, come, sit by me. Can't sleep? When I was ten, in our house in Madurai, I couldn't either. I'm your Ammamma Sangeeta, but back then I was a skinny girl lying on a mat, thinking, what if I fail the arithmetic test? What if Amma goes to the market and doesn't come back? Each what-if made my heart go faster.
One night my Amma noticed. She didn't scold. She sat by me, oiled my hair slowly and hummed a song, and after that she hummed the same song every night. She said, "I'm here. Tomorrow I'll be here too." The worries still came, but the song came first.
So, shall I oil your hair?

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta live when she was ten?
qa.a: In her family's house in Madurai.

qa.q: Why did young Sangeeta's heart go faster on the mat?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt frightened, because each what-if, like failing arithmetic or her Amma not coming back, felt like a real danger.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta's Amma made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Instead of scolding, she oiled Sangeeta's hair and hummed the same song every night with a simple promise to be there, giving a calm routine and reassurance.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel hearing that Ammamma once had the same worries?
qa.a: Gopika may feel less alone and less strange for lying awake, and more willing to try the hair-oiling ritual 🤍

grounding: A grandmother recalls her childhood what-ifs about failing and about her mother at bedtime, and how her mother's calm routine and reassurance softened them.

passage:
The week before my Class 11 chemistry unit test, I barely studied. That sounds lazy, but it didn't feel lazy. It felt like the opposite. I'm Deepika, and every evening I'd sit at the study table with the textbook open while my mind ran ahead: what if they ask the numericals I can't do? What if I blank on the periodic table? What if I get a low mark and Papa has to sign it? I thought, if I imagine every bad thing, at least I'm being careful.
By Thursday I'd done one page. My friend Farida came over and saw my notebook: a whole page of what-ifs, no equations. She didn't laugh. She just said, "Pick one what-if and study that." So we did numericals together for an hour. It was the first real hour all week.

qa.q: What did Farida see in Deepika's notebook?
qa.a: A whole page of what-ifs, no equations.

qa.q: Why did the constant what-ifs feel responsible rather than lazy to Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika believed that imagining every bad outcome was a way of being careful, so worrying felt like preparing even though almost no studying happened.

qa.q: What could Deepika try the next time the what-ifs start?
qa.a: Turn the biggest what-if into a task, like doing the numericals, and give it one focused hour, just as Farida suggested 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Farida to find a page of worries instead of equations?
qa.a: Farida could see a friend who was stuck rather than lazy, so instead of teasing, Farida offered a simple way in and studied alongside.

grounding: A teenager imagines every way a test could go wrong, which feels like being responsible but takes the place of studying until a friend helps turn one worry into work.

passage:
Tuition centre notes, Chetan sir, Class 12 physics batch, 3 February
Saurabh stayed back again today. He's bright and he works hard in class, but his practice sheets come back half empty. When I asked, it poured out: "Sir, what if the paper is lengthy? What if I get a bad centre? What if I don't clear the entrance and waste my parents' money?" He said he lies awake making lists of disasters and feels guilty if he stops, as if not worrying would be careless.
I told him his worry was doing a planner's job without actually planning. We took his biggest fear, a lengthy paper, and turned it into one action: a timed mock every Sunday. He wrote it in his diary. Next week I'll go through the first mock with him and see whether the sheets start to fill up.

qa.q: What action did Chetan and Saurabh turn the fear of a lengthy paper into?
qa.a: A timed mock every Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Saurabh feel guilty if he stops worrying?
qa.a: He feels that not worrying would be careless, as if the disaster lists are how he shows he takes the exam and his parents' money seriously.

qa.q: Why is a timed mock a better answer to Saurabh's fear than another list of disasters?
qa.a: It practises the very thing he fears, working against the clock, so it builds skill and confidence instead of only raising alarms.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's parents read his half-empty sheets if they didn't know about the worry?
qa.a: They might think he wasn't trying, when he was spending his energy on fear; knowing the truth could help them support him rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager lists every way an exam could go wrong and barely practises, because worrying feels responsible, until a teacher helps turn one fear into an action.

passage:
Aparna akka,
I'm leaving this under your door because it's easier than saying it at breakfast.
Since your final-year exams started, the house feels different. You check the gas, the door, your hall ticket, the alarm, again and again. And I've started doing it too. Last night I got out of bed twice to see if the back door was bolted. On the bus I keep checking my college ID even when I know it's in my bag. I didn't used to be like this.
I'm not angry. I know you're scared. The one evening we sat on the terrace and you told me honestly about the viva, I slept all night without checking anything. So can we try this? Dinner together at eight, no exam talk, and after that ten minutes where we both say how we really are. And only Appa checks the locks at night, once.

You asked about my family, so here's the strange part. The year my sister Afreen did her final year in pharmacy, I was nineteen, and I caught her worry like a cold. She'd refresh the university portal before breakfast, read her notes aloud at midnight, and ask Mum three times whether the internet bill was paid in case it cut out during the online exam. I told myself that was her thing. Then I started refreshing my own marks page, and I wasn't even in exams. I'd wake at four and check my phone for no reason.
What helped was boring. Mum put a timetable on the fridge: dinner at seven, lights out at eleven, phones in the kitchen. And one evening Afreen sat on my bed and said, "Zubin, I think I've been making you nervous too. I'm sorry." We talked for an hour. Honestly, that talk did more than anything.

qa.a: A timetable: dinner at seven, lights out at eleven, phones in the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Zubin start checking a marks page with no exams coming up?

qa.q: Which moment turned things around for Zubin, and why?
qa.a: Afreen sitting on the bed and admitting she had made Zubin nervous; that honest talk turned the tension into something shared instead of silently copied 🙂

qa.q: How might Afreen have seen her own habits after noticing Zubin?
qa.a: She may have realised her refreshing and late-night checking were spreading to Zubin, which is why she apologised and chose to talk openly.

grounding: A younger sibling picks up an anxious student's checking habits, and a clear home routine plus an honest talk lighten it.
